title: The Content of Imagined Sounds Changes Visual Motion Perception in the Cross-Bounce Illusion
authors: Christopher C. Berger & H. Henrik Ehrsson, 2017
research_question: Does the content of imagined sound change visual motion perception in a manner consistent with multisensory integration, specifically in the cross-bounce illusion?

participants.description: 72 healthy participants (24 per experiment, mean age Exp 1a=27.6, Exp 1b=24.5, Exp 2=26.1 years; mixed gender) recruited from the Stockholm area. No history of psychiatric/neurologic disorders, no hearing/vision problems.
participants.recruitment: student population in the Stockholm area

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two black discs (diameter = 0.702°) descending at a 45° angle, meeting at the center of a white square. Overlap conditions: 100% (complete overlap), 80% (partial overlap), 60% (partial overlap). Total duration 1500 ms, speed 10.081°/s.

Damped harmonic complex tone (200 ms, harmonics 1-10 of 250 Hz fundamental, amplitude linearly decreased from ±1 to ±0). Ramped harmonic complex tone (same as damped, played backwards). No sound condition.

measures.instrument: Self-report: 1-10 scale ('not at all' to 'extremely well and vividly')
Sensitivity index d' (derived from Hit rate and False-Alarm rate)
Response bias index c (derived from Hit rate and False-Alarm rate)

findings.antecedent: Imagined damped sound (vs. no sound) at moment discs meet
findings.mechanism: Multisensory integration of ecologically relevant imagined sound with ambiguous visual motion.
findings.quote: imagined damped sound significantly increased the probability of a bounce percept compared to the no-sound condition

findings.antecedent: Imagined ramped sound (vs. no sound) at moment discs meet
findings.mechanism: Lack of ecological relevance prevents multisensory integration.
findings.quote: imagined ramped sound did not (β=-0.05, SE=0.50, z=0.06, p=0.98)

findings.antecedent: Extent discs overlapped (higher percentage = more overlap)

findings.quote: significant negative relationship between the extent that the discs overlapped and the probability of a bounce percept

findings.antecedent: Imagined damped sound (vs. imagined ramped sound) at moment discs meet
findings.mechanism: Ecological relevance of damped sound promotes multisensory integration.

mechanisms: Multisensory integration: ecologically relevant imagined auditory stimuli are integrated with ambiguous visual stimuli, leading to changes in visual perception.
Unity assumption principle: only meaningful combinations of cross-modal sensory stimuli are integrated, explaining why damped (collision-like) sounds have an effect but ramped sounds do not.
Genuine perceptual phenomenon: the observed effect is not attributable to changes in attention or response bias, as demonstrated by the sensitivity and bias indices.
moderators: Vividness of auditory imagery: higher vividness leads to a stronger imagery-induced cross-bounce illusion.
implementation_implications: What people imagine hearing can change what they see, suggesting that mental imagery can influence real-world perception.
The findings support the notion that auditory imagery and auditory perception involve overlapping neural representations.
limitations: Previous studies on imagery-induced cross-bounce illusion (e.g., Berger & Ehrsson, 2013) had less robust controls for attention and post-perceptual effects, which this study aimed to improve upon.
Future neuroimaging experiments are needed to investigate whether the imagery-induced cross-bounce illusion involves the same multisensory areas as the classic cross-bounce illusion.

paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractCan what we imagine hearing change what we see? Whether imagined sensory stimuli are integrated with external sensory stimuli to shape our perception of the world has only recently begun to come under scrutiny. Here, we made use of the cross-bounce illusion in which an auditory stimulus presented at the moment two passing objects meet promotes the perception that the objects bounce off rather than cross by one another to examine whether the content of imagined sound changes visual motion perception in a manner that is consistent with multisensory integration. The results from this study revealed that auditory imagery of a sound with acoustic properties typical of a collision (i.e., damped sound) promoted the bounce-percept, but auditory imagery of the same sound played backwards (i.e., ramped sound) did not. Moreover, the vividness of the participants’ auditory imagery predicted the strength of this imagery-induced illusion. In a separate experiment, we ruled out the possibility that changes in attention (i.e., sensitivity index d′) or response bias (response bias index c) were sufficient to explain this effect. Together, these findings suggest that this imagery-induced multisensory illusion reflects the successful integration of real and imagined cross-modal sensory stimuli, and more generally, that what we imagine hearing can change what we see.
